The new Civil Code does not contain a specific article that provides for the 
defaulting party to undo the effects of a breach. This is in contrast with old art­
icle 1143, which provided that ‘a promisee can request that what has been done in 
breach of the obligation be destroyed; and he can request authorisation to destroy 
it himself at the expense of the defaulting promisor’.50 The Code now only provides, 
in new article 1222, for the latter type. This enables the injured party to obtain court 
approval to destroy a non-​compliant subject-​matter of the contract and claim the 
cost of doing so from the defaulting party.51 It is, however, widely understood that 
the injured party can, as before the reforms, seek in court that the defaulting party 
themselves undo the breach.52
(iii)  Situations in which specific enforcement of non-​monetary obligations will not 
be ordered
There are three situations in which specific enforcement is unavailable in French 
law. The first is where performance is impossible.53 This might occur, for example, 
where the subject-​matter of the contract has already been purchased by a bona fide 
third party.54 The second is where specific enforcement would result in involuntary 
servitude, such as in a contract for the provision of personal services. It has there­
fore been refused in respect of a contract in which an artist was commissioned to 
paint and deliver a picture.55 The third is where there is a ‘manifest disproportion’ 
between the cost of performance to the defaulting party and the interest of the in­
jured party in obtaining it.56
This exception is new and amongst the most notable changes made by the re­
forms. Previously, the courts did not have any discretion as to whether to grant 
specific enforcement. An order could not be resisted on grounds of unreasonable­
ness or disproportionality. Nor was there an undue hardship bar, meaning that the 
remedy could be obtained even at the financial ruin of the defaulting party.57
